e.t: Abelmain is a proper name, rendered as “Abelmain” or “Avelmen.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 16:4. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name’s precise significance in that account cannot be explained here; its basic lexical function is simply to designate the named entity called Abelmain.

This noun means “ignorance”: a state of not knowing or lacking understanding. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe a person’s uninformed condition rather than a specific action. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Samuel, Chronicles, Ecclesiastes, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains ignorance or lack of knowledge.

This Greek LXX verb means “next of kin.” As a verb, it describes someone functioning in the role of a close family relative rather than simply naming that relative. The word occurs 32 times in 21 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, with many occurrences in Ruth and Numbers. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “prize of contest,” referring to the reward gained by someone who competes and succeeds. It presents achievement as something awarded after a struggle or contest, rather than merely an object or possession. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and comparison being made.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Aitham” or “Etham.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah: Jeremiah 27:44 and Jeremiah 30:13. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish whether it identifies a person, place, or another named entity in each passage.

This noun refers to one who speaks riddles—someone whose words express meaning indirectly through puzzling or enigmatic speech. It describes a speaker rather than the riddle itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, at Numbers 21:27. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a person who communicates in riddles. This noun means “ostentation; pretension”: an outward display that presents a person or thing as more impressive, important, or capable than it truly is. It describes showy self-importance rather than simple confidence or honor. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs seven times, in Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is boastful display or affected importance.

This Greek LXX adjective means “unchewed,” describing something that has not been chewed. It refers to the physical condition of food or another substance before chewing has taken place, rather than expressing an action or a person’s character. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Job 20:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: something is still unchewed.

gl: taking in on all sides; widespreading
d: taking in on all sides; widespreading

e.t: This adjective describes something that takes in all sides or spreads widely. It presents an image of broad reach or encompassing extent, rather than something narrow or confined. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), in Wisdom 17:17, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains the idea of something widespreading or extending around and across what it touches.

This adverb describes acting “impudently” or in an “ungodly” way—without proper reverence or restraint. It points to the manner of a person’s conduct rather than naming the person or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 21:29. Its core meaning describes conduct marked by shameless boldness or disregard for God. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “spring up; rise.” It describes something coming up or appearing from below, and it can be used for natural growth or the rising of something into view. The word occurs 57 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its basic idea is used across many kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is rising and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “exchanging; requital”—the idea of giving something in return or receiving a corresponding response. It describes an act of repayment or exchange rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Psalm 118:112. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense centers on something returned or exchanged in response to something else.

Antipatros is a proper name, used to identify a person rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees. The name appears at 1 Maccabees 12:16 and 14:22. Without the surrounding verse text, these references establish where the name occurs but do not by themselves identify which person is meant or explain that person’s role in the passage.

This verb means “dismiss”: it describes sending someone away or refusing to keep them present. It can therefore express a deliberate act of removal or rejection, depending on the sentence in which it appears. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, in Psalms, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Arema is a proper name, also rendered Arima. It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Judges 9:41. The available meaning information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough context to determine whether Arema refers to a person, settlement, or another named entity in that passage.

Asebōn, also rendered Asevon, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings. The supplied lexical information preserves the name rather than giving it a descriptive meaning such as an action, quality, or object. It appears 83 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across 82 verses, with many occurrences in Proverbs and additional occurrences in Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its specific identity or role must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to a mole, described also as a blind rat. It names a small burrowing animal rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 11:30, within a list of animals. Its basic meaning is therefore a particular kind of underground-dwelling creature, with “mole” serving as the clear English rendering in that occurrence.

This adjective means “austere,” describing something marked by strictness, severity, or little softness. It functions as a describing word rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 14:30. The verse text is not available in this record, so the word’s precise force in that sentence cannot be stated from the word alone. Its central meaning remains a quality that is stern, restrained, or severe.

Achalia, also called Akhalia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah: once in Nehemiah 1:1 and again in Nehemiah 10:2. The available information identifies it as the name itself, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or significance. Its meaning in either passage therefore depends on identifying the individual in the surrounding biblical context.

Apsalōmos is a proper name, referring to an individual called Apsalōmos (also rendered Apsalomos). The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 1 Maccabees: 1 Maccabees 11:70 and 13:11. Since the available information identifies the name but does not include the surrounding verse text, its particular role in either passage must be understood from the immediate context. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object.

This word is a proper name, referring to Beeri, also rendered Viri. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Hosea 1:1. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand the person’s role in that setting. Its precise significance therefore remains that of a personal name within the biblical genealogy or historical reference where it appears.

Gabathon is a proper name for a place, rendered in English as “Gabathōn” or “Gavathon.” It is a Greek LXX place name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. The name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, across three verses in 1 Kings 15–16. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, its specific role in each passage cannot be explained further; its lexical meaning is the place name itself.

Gedour, also rendered Yethur, is a proper name—the name of a specific person or place in the Greek Old Testament wording. Its precise referent is not identified by the lexical information alone, so the surrounding passage is needed to determine whom or what it names. This LXX word occurs twice, in 1 Chronicles 8:31 and 1 Chronicles 9:37, showing that it is a specific name rather than a general description or action.

This word means “knee,” the joint in the middle of the leg where the thigh and lower leg meet. It is a noun naming this part of the body, whether referring to one knee or to knees generally. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 28 times, including passages from Genesis, Deuteronomy, Judges, Kings, Isaiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its ordinary meaning remains the physical body part; the surrounding verse determines what action or situation involving the knee is being described.

This adjective describes something as ten cubits long, giving its length as a precise measurement. It does not name an object, action, or person; it describes a dimension. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Kings 7:47. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, while the surrounding context identifies what measured object is being described.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a measure or the act of measuring something out. It is used for determining or assigning dimensions, quantities, or portions rather than describing the object itself. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, including passages in 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being measured and the surrounding wording.

This adjective describes someone or something as eminent or distinguished—standing out as notably excellent, honored, or prominent. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense is clear: marked out by distinction or outstanding quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “way through” or “thoroughfare”—a route that allows people to pass from one place to another. It can describe a physical passage or roadway rather than the journey itself. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including passages from Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Proverbs, Wisdom, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains an accessible route or passage through an area.

This word means “oak,” referring to a strong, established tree. It is a noun used for an oak tree or a place identified by one. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times across 16 verses, showing that oak trees are mentioned in several different settings rather than in only one passage. The word appears from Genesis through Zechariah, including references associated with recognizable places and landmarks. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an oak tree.

Ether is a proper name, referring to a person named Ether rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Joshua 19:7. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its broader role in that passage cannot be explained here. The name should therefore be understood simply as the personal designation Ether, with the specific reference identifying where this person is mentioned.

This Greek LXX verb means “throw out”: to cast something or someone out from a place or group. It describes an act of expelling rather than merely moving something. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including Nehemiah and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being expelled and the surrounding passage.

This verb means “bring forth”: to produce, cause something to come out, or make it appear. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 55:10, so its normal biblical use is represented by that single occurrence. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what is being brought forth there; the word itself supplies the basic idea of producing or bringing something forward.

This noun means “destruction”: the ruin or complete bringing down of something. It names an outcome rather than an action, pointing to what is destroyed or the condition produced by devastating loss. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Numbers 32:21 and once in Deuteronomy 4:26. Those references locate its use, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular situation in each passage. Its central sense remains destruction.

Eleazar is a personal name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears 82 times and is consistently rendered “Eleazar.” The name occurs throughout the Old Testament portion of this corpus and also in later Greek writings. Because it is a proper name, its specific referent depends on the passage where it appears; the name itself identifies the person being mentioned.

This verb means “listen to,” describing the act of giving attention to what someone says. It expresses hearing with directed attention rather than merely receiving a sound. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nahum 1:12. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the attentive act of listening to someone or something spoken.

This verb means “give ear”—to listen attentively or turn one’s attention toward what is being said. It describes an active response to speech, whether the speaker is addressing a person or calling for careful attention. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 35 times, showing repeated use for the act of listening. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and speaker.

“Object of malignant joy” refers to a person or thing that becomes the target of another’s cruel delight. As a noun, it names someone or something treated as a cause for malicious pleasure rather than genuine rejoicing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX word, it occurs four times: once in Exodus and three times in Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea is being made an object of harmful, spiteful enjoyment.

This Greek verb means “come” or “go,” describing movement from one place to another. Its exact direction depends on the sentence: it can describe someone arriving, approaching, or departing. In the Greek Old Testament, it is a common action word, appearing 935 times across 888 verses. It is used throughout the translated Hebrew Scriptures and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense remains broad and practical rather than tied to one special kind of movement. The surrounding words determine whether “come” or “go” best expresses the action.

gl: easily satisfied; contented with one's food
d: easily satisfied; contented with one's food

e.t: This Greek LXX adjective describes someone who is easily satisfied, especially with the food available. It expresses contentment rather than demanding more or seeking greater variety. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 15:3, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains a person whose appetite is modest and readily contented. Scripture presents this as a description of what someone is like, not as an action being performed.

gl: at one's own fireside; at home
d: at one's own fireside; at home

e.t: This adjective describes something connected with one’s own home or fireside—something familiar, domestic, or belonging in the household. It can refer to being “at home” or “at one’s own fireside,” emphasizing a person’s immediate household setting rather than a public or distant place. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 37:11. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely how the adjective functions there, but its basic sense remains a connection with home and one’s own household.

This verb means to make something tame or to restrain it. It describes bringing something under control rather than leaving it wild, uncontrolled, or unchecked. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 16:18. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being restrained in that passage, but the word itself centers on taming or holding back. Its direct meaning is therefore practical and controlling: making something manageable or limiting its force.

Thalabin is a proper name, rendered in the gloss as “Thalabin” or “Thalavin.” It does not function like an ordinary descriptive word; it identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX, at Judges 1:35. Without the verse text and surrounding context, it is not possible to establish whether the name refers to a person, place, or another named entity.

Iekthiel, also rendered Iekthil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:18. The name itself is identified by these two renderings, but no further lexical definition is given. Its significance in that passage therefore comes from the surrounding genealogy and verse context, not from a general abstract meaning.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Iessaimou” or “Iessemu.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in 1 Samuel, in references concerning the same named person or designation. The name appears in 1 Samuel 23:19, 23:24, 26:1, and 26:3. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is simply to identify a person by name.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ioudaismos” or “Iuthezmos.” It identifies a named subject rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times across four verses, appearing in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Because no verse text or English rendering is available, its more precise force in any particular passage cannot be stated from the word alone.

Ionatham is a proper name, rendered as “Iōnatham” or “Ionatham.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Judges 18:30. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding passage is needed to understand the person’s role and significance in that verse. The spelling may appear slightly different in English, but these forms represent the same personal name.

This verb means “sit down,” describing the action of taking a seated position. It is a straightforward action word rather than a title or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse, showing ordinary use across several books. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage. The word’s basic meaning remains the act of sitting down or becoming seated.

This adjective describes something that reaches as far as the wrist. It gives a physical measure of length or extent rather than naming an object by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 13:19. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its exact application in that verse cannot be stated more specifically. Its basic meaning remains clear: reaching to, or extending as far as, the wrist.

This adjective means “quite,” expressing a strong degree or extent in the sentence where it appears. It describes or qualifies something rather than naming an action, person, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. The exact force of the adjective in that verse is best understood from the surrounding wording, but its basic role is to intensify or qualify the statement it accompanies.

Keilam is a proper name, also rendered Kilam. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 15:44. The word functions as a name rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its specific referent in that passage cannot be explained further. Its basic lexical meaning is therefore the personal or place-name Keilam, with Kilam as an approved alternate rendering.

This word means an “exhortation” or “command”: a spoken urging that calls someone to act or obey. It is a noun, so it names the exhortation or command itself rather than the action of giving it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 30:27. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how this command functions there, but the word itself points to a clear directive or earnest appeal.

Kore is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies individuals in genealogical, family, and narrative settings. The name occurs 43 times across 42 verses in this corpus, with especially frequent use in Numbers and Psalms. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who is being named. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which person named Kore is intended in a particular passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “cry” or “outcry”—a vocal expression that is heard or raised aloud. It can describe a person’s cry, a collective outcry, or a forceful appeal, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs 60 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used broadly rather than referring to one particular kind of sound. Its recorded uses include Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, Esther, and other books.

The word is the proper name “Kōs,” also given as “Kos.” It identifies a named place rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times: twice in 1 Chronicles and once in 1 Maccabees. The lexical information provides the name itself, while the surrounding verse determines what is being said about Kos in each passage.

This noun means an advantage or benefit—something that brings help, gain, or usefulness. It refers to the positive value obtained from an action, situation, or arrangement. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:27. The word’s basic sense remains focused on what is beneficial or profitable, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is described as beneficial there.

Marisan is a proper name, functioning as a name rather than as a general description, action, or quality. Its meaning is the name itself, “Marisan,” and the available information does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in 2 Chronicles 11:8 and once in 1 Maccabees 5:66. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what the name identifies in either passage.

Massourouth, also rendered Massuruth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not establish whether the name refers to a place, person, or another location-related designation. It occurs twice in the Greek text of Numbers, in Numbers 33:30 and 33:31. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding passage and the underlying Hebrew naming tradition.

gl: mixed with purple; decorated with purple
d: mixed with purple; decorated with purple

e.t: This word describes something mixed with purple or decorated with purple. It can function as a descriptive word for a purple-mixed or purple-adorned object, and it appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Isaiah 3. Its basic sense points to purple as part of an object’s coloring or decoration. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the particular item being described, but the word itself centers on purple mixture or ornamentation.

This word means “hired hand,” referring to a person employed to work for pay. It describes someone serving in a working role because he has been hired, rather than identifying him as the owner or head of the household. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 17 times across 17 verses, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, and Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

This noun refers to “man's appointed doom; fate”—the destiny or outcome appointed for a person. It presents fate as something allotted or awaiting someone, rather than describing an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs seven times, chiefly in 3 Maccabees and also in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains an appointed fate or doom.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Naēm” or “Nem.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or idea. In the Greek LXX text, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:19. Because the word functions as a name, its basic meaning is the person it identifies, while the surrounding passage is needed to explain that person’s place in the genealogy or narrative. The name itself does not provide a broader doctrinal or descriptive meaning.

This Greek LXX particle means “sure as,” expressing a firm, emphatic affirmation. It strengthens a statement by presenting it as certain rather than doubtful. The word is brief and functions as a particle, so it does not name a person, object, or action; instead, it adds force to what is being asserted. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis 42, showing a limited recorded use in this corpus.

This verb means to “scrape” or “plane”—to remove material from a surface by rubbing or cutting against it. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, so its basic sense is narrowly represented in this corpus. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to scraping or smoothing a surface.

This noun means “acknowledgment” or “agreement”: recognizing something openly or expressing shared understanding. It can describe an affirmation or a settled accord between people. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, showing that it is an occasional term rather than a dominant expression. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject matter.

This Greek LXX noun means “loins” or “waist,” referring to the lower part of the torso. It names a physical body area rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 61 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, so it is a recurring bodily term across these writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the waist or loins.

gl: leave on one side; leave remaining
d: leave on one side; leave remaining

e.t: This verb means “leave on one side” or “leave remaining.” It describes the act of passing something by, setting it aside, or allowing something to remain after other things have been removed. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees 1:19–20. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine which aspect—setting aside or leaving remaining—is emphasized in each occurrence.

This verb means “trample”: to step forcefully on something or someone, pressing it underfoot. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, so it is a recurring action word, though its exact force in any passage depends on what is being trampled and the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains forceful stepping underfoot.

This word means “sandals,” referring to footwear worn on the feet. It is a noun naming the item itself, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Habakkuk 3:5. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s ordinary meaning is the sandals a person wears. This sense remains simple and concrete: a type of open footwear. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L710213:identity; p03:word:lxx:L710213:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L710213:reference:0]

This verb means “circumcise”: to perform circumcision on someone. It describes a physical act that appears throughout the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. In this LXX entity, it occurs 38 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through 4 Maccabees. Its use includes passages concerning individuals and groups, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word itself identifies the act rather than explaining the reason, covenant significance, or personal response connected with it.

This noun means a “wanderer,” describing a person who moves from place to place rather than remaining settled in one location. It is a personal designation, not an action word or description of a place. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Job 2:9, so its ordinary sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here.

This noun means “privilege”: a special right, honor, or advantage granted to someone. It refers to a recognized position or benefit rather than an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs twice, once in Psalms and once in 3 Maccabees, showing that its basic sense is used across both books. The surrounding verse determines what particular privilege is meant, but the word itself points to an honored right or benefit belonging to a person or group.

This word means “expectation”—the forward-looking anticipation of what is believed or awaited. As a noun, it names an anticipated outcome rather than the act of expecting itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages from Genesis, Psalms, and Isaiah as well as later Jewish books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains expectation directed toward what is yet to come.

This Greek verb means “look at” or “behold”—directing attention toward someone or something. It describes the act of seeing attentively, whether simply observing or taking notice. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Job and once in Wisdom. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains deliberate looking or observing.

This adjective means “fire-breathing,” describing something that breathes out or is associated with fire. It presents fire as issuing from the thing being described, rather than merely being near it or resembling its heat. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, in Wisdom 11:18. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise referent in that verse cannot be described further, but its basic sense remains a vivid description connected with breathing fire.

“Rouma” or “Rhuma” is a proper name, identifying a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 23:36. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to determine whether the reference there is to a location or a person. Its precise referent therefore depends on the context of that passage.

Rōgellim, also rendered Rhoyellim, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named place or entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in 2 Samuel: 17:27 and 19:32. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific geographical or narrative significance cannot be stated more precisely, but its basic function is clear: it names Rōgellim.

Samarath is a proper name, rendered as “Samarath.” It does not function as a common word describing an object, action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:21. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, its particular identity and role in that genealogy cannot be explained further from this word entry alone.

This word is a proper name rendered “Sarouia” or “Saroia.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across seven verses, all in 1 Chronicles. Because it is a personal name, its precise reference in any passage depends on the surrounding genealogy or narrative. The name appears from 1 Chronicles 2 through 1 Chronicles 27, showing repeated use in Chronicles’ historical records.

Sēli, also rendered Sili, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 11:8.
